title: Loopy Farm 🚜 - Lessons and data from development after launch.
author: MrJurasek
selftext:
Hey there, fellow builders and gamers! 🚜🚜🚜

A couple of months ago, I posted here about the launch of my farming game Loopy Farm. The game is fully developed with AI. Since then, life got busy on many fronts, so I had less time available for development, but I did not stall and somehow managed to publish 11 updates since the release of 1.0.

Today, I released a major update with the implementation of Seasons, which is a recurring LiveOps feature that brings new strategic aspects to the gameplay.

On this occasion, I wanted to share with you some more lessons from this solo development journey.

Data from Loopy Farm so far:

\- Currently around 80 registrations.

\- Some players are still coming back to the game repeatedly weeks after registration, which is an amazing feeling and shows some retention signals! (even though the dataset is very limited to draw any conclusions)

\- 4 payments (3 from my friends and 1 from the player I do not know 🥹).

\- Didn't run any campaigns yet, just tried posting mainly on Reddit here and there. This community building has proven to be more difficult than I originally expected.

\- A lot of technical debt for sure.



My lessons and tips (note: I'm using Claude Code and I have experience as a UX designer and Game Designer):

\- \*AI as a GAME DESIGN sparring partner\*: Proved to me as a great sparring partner for the game design discussions before the actual game development. Now anytime I start a new feature, I start in planning mode, where I share my ideas to get challenged or to get another perspective. I know it has its shortcomings and limitations, but in some cases these new perspectives helped me to steer my original idea to a better direction.

\- SUPER SECRET NEGLECTED TIP: AI is great at building tools for your game. As designers, we should be doing this more often. In my case, it helped me build economy models for various gameplay stages, balance calculators, etc.

\- SUPER SECRET NEGLECTED TIP 2: After each important game design session, use the AI to create a summary of the feature for you. Since the AI has context and code available, it can help you keep your specifications always up-to-date. Take it to your advantage. Anytime in the future you will revisit something, you will be thanking me for this practice.

\- Fable was a significant help in the optimisation efforts of my game. Before, the performance on mobile wasn't there. Now, with a few optimisation rounds, I managed to progress, and the Android version is almost ready.

\- \*SKIN IN THE GAME ASAP\* - As long as you are not building the game just for yourself -> Try to publish your game with the target audience as soon as possible and start collecting feedback. You can even see it here on Reddit. Sometimes just a trailer before the actual demo can help you collect amazing feedback and build a community. (I'm guilty on this one, and should have gone public much much sooner)

\- Following on the lesson above -> Building the first user base of players? The truth is, you can't just rely on the "virality" of your game only. Sure, there are cases where it happens, but simply having a good game is unfortunately not enough. Marketing is not something that you do after. It should be part of the process from day 1.

\- Use your early builds as a source for the feedback. Either by directly talking with your players or by a structured feedback form. Just a simple "What do you think" post is a missed opportunity.

Got any questions? Do not hesitate to ask or reach out via DM.



Interested in the game itself? You can test it out at [loopyfarm.com](http://loopyfarm.com/)

Follow the journey at [https://www.reddit.com/r/loopyfarm/](https://www.reddit.com/r/loopyfarm/)

comments.author: OinkLikeAPig
comments.body:
It looks amazing, smooth and definitely something I would try. Well done.

So based on your personal skills, I guess you are solid on the graphical aspects. I am really onyl technical and got hyped yesterday making a picture to a 3D model in segments yesterday. Could you elborate on your process of thinking about a tractor fx. to actually have it in the game?

Also, the neglected tip #1 - when do you stop up and think “this needs to be a tool”?

replies.author: MrJurasek
replies.body:
Thanks! You can already check it out on the link provided in the post. Happy farming! 🧑‍🌾   
Actually I do not consider myself that solid in the graphics, but over those years I learnt to think mostly in the production scope and the limits within the existing situation. What do I mean by that? The game is always a mirror of the skills and resources. Resources can be split into time (time invested and deadlines) and finances. 

Now how does it translate to reality in my case?

I am a solo developer, with limited time and budget. How does it translate to Loopy Farm?

So basically I'm happy that game exists, because without AI it would just stay as a concept on the paper, but it doesn't look nowhere near from my vision. And that is completely OK :)  


One example: Machines in the game.  
\- I would love to have this game in 3D or Iso, but 2D was much easier technically and production wise to create.

\- Now that I have them in 2D -> I would love to have the machines rendered from 3/4 perspective. But that would require me to draw each machine in 8 directions. Since I plan to add dozens and dozens of new machines, that would kill the development completely.

\- I can see myself using RIVE to animate all of these existing machines, but that might increase the performance costs and once again, takes a significant amount of production time from my part (I would need to increase my animation skills a lot)

\- My machines are currently using just a basic particles. Why? Once again -> Selected tech and limited tech knowledge on my part. I also keep in mind that I want to get on mobile soon where the performance is even more limited.

\- After having a chat with few of the existing players, I found out, that despite my original intention to have a strong focus on machines, they care more about actual production and farm. Therefore, the current design is in a "good enough" state for now. Will revisit in the future.

  
Another good example is a Behance or Dribbble and UI design. Those websites are full of extremely attractive case studies and experimental UIs, but in reality they never hit the production. Most of those designs would be killed by PM or budget. Even if any of those designs were to be approved, then the harsh reality of development would come and most of the stuff wouldn't be possible.

So with all that, I would suggest to start small and experiment step-by-step. Consistency and small steps will get you in to a new places in no time.

replies.author: OinkLikeAPig
replies.body:
Thanks for the detailed answer. Most of it is also how I think. Especially the limitations and whats within. Soon have a base game thats good enough, and created the project with basic sprites to be replaced.  
I had a 6 month course during my studies 5 years ago in game development, and I loved it. It is still hard to understand how productive AI can be working solo.

Will look into your recommendations and thanks again.

comments.author: TradeNPlayz
comments.body: Looks pretty nice. Did you already have prior experience in game design/dev before starting this?

replies.author: MrJurasek
replies.body:
Thanks and yes. I work in mobile gaming for over a decade and I had a chance to work on a couple of projects from the 0 to release (as a UX designer, Game Designer and even Lead Game Designer).   
  
That previous experience helped, but doing it solo is a whole different sport. I admit - I bit off a bit more than I could chew for the start.  
When creating a new project, there are always new challenges that have no template you can re-use, so the having a clear creative workflow always helps.   
  
If you are interested, you can check my first prompt, which started it all. See my previous post here:  
[https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1sf9u0r/i\_made\_a\_first\_prompt\_guide\_how\_to\_start\_making/](https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1sf9u0r/i_made_a_first_prompt_guide_how_to_start_making/)

replies.author: TradeNPlayz
replies.body:
Thanks! I saved both of your posts!

Can you possibly recommend any free online resources for a beginner to get started in game design? I'm looking to develop my own game with AI too.

replies.author: MrJurasek
replies.body:
Sure! It depends on what kind of game you want to start building, but you can never go wrong with youtube videos from Game Maker's Toolkit and Extra Credits.

If you are getting started, I suggest to start small and then step-by-step iterate and expand. The "feature creep" is a real thing and it can easily lead to burn out, stalling and all kinds of frustrations that will end up with the unfinished game. "Done is better than perfect" is a cliché, but it will help you to keep the momentum. Good luck!
